title: Won Buddhism
hook: a Korean Buddhism of the twentieth century centered on a simple circle

segments.voice: Yesterday, the insight movement, lay teachers in rented rooms. Your line was insight at home. Which chore did you name to yourself as you did it? Day one thousand three hundred forty-eight.

On the altar there is no statue. No seated figure, no gold, no face. There is a circle: a plain black ring on a white field, framed and hung where a Buddha image might be. People bow to it. They sit facing it in silence. They chant before it on a Sunday morning, in Seoul or in a converted house in an American suburb. A child in the back row might ask what it's a picture of, and the answer would take a while. Today: Won Buddhism.
screen: `NO STATUE ON THE ALTAR.` → `A PLAIN BLACK RING.` → `WHAT IS IT A PICTURE OF?`

segments.voice: First, the beginning. Won Buddhism is a modern Korean Buddhism. Its founder is known to his followers as Sotaesan. Tradition says he spent years searching for the truth without a teacher, questioning and struggling, until he awakened. Afterward he read the Buddhist scriptures and recognized his own awakening in the Buddha's teaching, and he founded a new community. Won is the Korean word for circle. Second, the circle itself. It is called Il-Won-Sang, the One Circle image. Won Buddhists explain it as a symbol of the dharmakaya, the truth-body of the Buddha: the original nature of all beings and the source of everything. It is not a picture of a person. It is a picture of what is already whole, before anyone draws a line through it. That is why it stands on the altar where a statue would be. Third, what follows from that. If the one truth is everywhere, then, in a phrase Won Buddhists use, everywhere is a Buddha image, and every act is an offering to the Buddha. Your coworker, your child, the person in line at the pharmacy: each is treated as a place to meet the Buddha. Work and family are not interruptions of practice. They are where practice happens. Won Buddhists speak of timeless Zen and placeless Zen: meditation that does not wait for the right hour or the right room. Fourth, the purpose. The founder's motto, in a paraphrase, is that as material civilization opens up, a spiritual civilization should open up with it. So Won Buddhism runs schools and charities alongside its temples, and its ministers, women and men alike, serve congregations that meet on ordinary weekends. All of it circles back to one plain ring on a white wall.
screen: `A MODERN KOREAN BUDDHISM.` · `IL-WON-SANG, THE ONE CIRCLE.` · `EVERYWHERE A BUDDHA IMAGE.` · `SPIRIT TO MATCH THE MATERIAL.` · then, large: `THE CIRCLE.`

segments.voice: If you have paper and a pen, draw one circle, in a single motion, without lifting the pen. Don't fix it, even if it wobbles. If there's no paper, trace one slowly in the air with your finger. Now rest your eyes on it. Notice the inside, the outside, and the line between them. Let your breath go around with it, in and out, beginning and ending in the same place. Let it stand, for these few moments, for something whole. The bell holds the time.
Won Buddhism. A modern Korean Buddhism founded by Sotaesan, whose altar holds a plain circle, the One Circle image of the truth that is everywhere. Today's word.

Your line: the circle. Today, when you see something round, a cup's rim, a clock, a wheel, let it remind you to treat the next person you meet as a place to meet something whole. Day one thousand three hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Won Buddhists enshrine the Il-Won-Sang, a plain circle, on their altars instead of a Buddha statue, meet for weekly services with meditation and chanting, and aim to practice anywhere and at any time, treating all things as a Buddha and every act as an offering.

fork.reveal: a plain circle, the One Circle image: a picture of the truth that is already whole, everywhere, not a picture of a person.

original.note: Korean Il-Won-Sang, the One Circle image (in Chinese characters 一圓相), at the center of Won Buddhist altars.

trapdoor: what you thought: the circle is a logo.
what it means: the Il-Won-Sang, set on the altar in place of a statue, as the truth that is everywhere.
what a scholar hears: the dharmakaya pictured as a circle, and the teaching that everywhere is a Buddha image and every act an offering.

notes: The index hook says 'of the twentieth century'; the voice says only 'modern' under the claims rule.
Sotaesan's search 'without a teacher' and his later recognition of his awakening in the Buddhist scriptures is given as 'tradition says': confirm.
Gloss 'won, the Korean word for circle' and Il-Won-Sang as 'One Circle image': confirm.
Phrases 'everywhere a Buddha image, every act an offering' (cheocheo bulsang, sasa bulgong) and 'timeless Zen, placeless Zen' paraphrased: confirm wording.
Founding motto paraphrased, not quoted; ministers (kyomu) described as 'women and men alike': confirm.
Original-language entry uses Korean hangul with Hanja in the note rather than Devanagari; confirm 일원상 / 一圓相.
Hook mentions a service in Seoul and in a converted American suburban house as illustration, not specific temples.
